summary: The note describes how community college adult education programs have grown since September 2023 to serve working adults through flexible formats, business partnerships, financial aid, and continually updated curricula. It gives examples from several named colleges and quotes from a student, a dean, and a policy analyst. It also covers challenges such as limited funding and technological change, and concludes that lifelong learning and ongoing innovation will drive future success.
one_line: Community colleges are expanding flexible, job-aligned, financially supported adult education programs that promote lifelong learning despite funding and technology challenges.
key_facts: In October 2023, Central Valley Community College in California launched a six-month certification program in cybersecurity in response to demand for IT security professionals.

John Thompson, a 45-year-old veteran, studies in the online business administration program at Lakeside Community College and says online study "has been a lifesaver" alongside a fulltime job and family.

Marsha Singh, Dean of Adult Education at Riverbend Community College, describes partnerships as a reciprocal relationship that fills talent gaps for local employers and gives students real-world skills.
Smithtown Community College and the local hospital system collaborated on a tailored nursing assistant program that feeds directly into hospital staffing needs.
In December 2023, Gateway Community College announced a scholarship fund for adults returning to college that covers up to 75% of tuition for qualified applicants.
In March 2024, Harbor City Community College revamped its entire adult education catalog, adding programs in renewable energy technologies and health information management.
Community colleges offer evening and weekend classes as well as online and hybrid courses to fit adult learners' schedules.
Many community colleges have increased counseling services, tutoring, and career guidance for adult learners.
Committees of faculty, industry experts, and adult education specialists regularly review and update course offerings.
Many community colleges have implemented learning communities and alumni networks to foster continuous improvement and keep former students engaged.
Community colleges face challenges including limited funding, changing demographic trends, and the need to keep pace with technological change.
Dr. Emily Rosenthal, a policy analyst specializing in adult education, says community colleges are adept at "adjusting their sails to meet the winds of change."
